title: The Pitt and ER are similar enough for lawsuit to proceed, judge rules
description: US drama The Pitt is similar enough to medical series ER for a lawsuit against its producers to progress, a court in the US has ruled. The widow of Mi
body: US drama The Pitt is similar enough to medical series ER for a lawsuit against its producers to progress, a court in the US has ruled. The widow of Michael Crichton, who created ER, argues The Pitt is effectively a reboot of the series, which has been made without proper permission or credit. Sherri Crichton says her husband's contract included a "frozen rights" provision that prohibited any spin-offs, sequels or reboots of ER being made without his express consent.A three-judge panel said there are "clear and numerous similarities between The Pitt and ER," which means the case can go ahead. Warner Bros previously described the lawsuit as "baseless" and sought to have it dismissed.Listing the similarities between the two shows, the court cited the emergency room setting, the fast pace, use of medical jargon, graphic depictions of injuries, and younger doctors fresh from medical school being trained. "We find the details here suffice for a prima facie case," the judges said.It means the case will now go to a jury trial in Los Angeles Superior Court.But the judges dismissed separate claims against actor-producer Noah Wyle, executive producer John Wells and showrunner R Scott Gemmill.The justices said there was insufficient evidence to show the three producers were aware they could be violating Crichton's contractual rights.ER launched in 1994, based on original screenplay written by Crichton. It starred George Clooney, Anthony Edwards, Eriq La Salle and Maria Bello, and aired 331 episodes over the next 15 years.The show, which followed a group of doctors working in an emergency room in Chicago, was a hit with viewers and critics, and won 23 Emmy Awards during its run including outstanding drama series.Discussions about a possible reboot of the show began in 2020, and studio Warner Bros spent months negotiating with Crichton's estate.Those talks were reported to have collapsed over credit and financial guarantees, and producers began developing The Pitt in its place.But Sherri Crichton and the John Michael Crichton Trust argue the show is a rebranded but uncredited reboot of ER, using the same formula, pacing, style and setting, rather than an entirely original series. They said producers "simply moved the show from Chicago to Pittsburgh, rebranded it The Pitt, and ploughed ahead without any attribution or compensation for Crichton and his heirs". Many actors and creatives from ER also work on The Pitt, including Wyle, Gemmill and Wells.After legal action began in 2024, Warner Bros Television said in a statement that the lawsuit was "baseless", arguing that The Pitt was a "new and original show", adding that the studio would "vigorously defend against these meritless claims".But in a 33-page opinion published on Wednesday, a three-judge panel unanimously upheld an earlier ruling that Crichton's estate had presented enough evidence to pursue its claim. Warner Bros had sought to have the lawsuit dismissed on appeal, arguing the shows shared only "generic similarities" common to "any dramatic story involving emergency room doctors".The judges said they had compared the opening episode scripts for the two shows and found sufficient similarities in plot, themes, dialogue, mood, setting, pace, characters, graphic injury detail and sequence of events. Sherri Crichton said: "I am deeply gratified by the Court of Appeal decision and look forward to discovery and to our case, which affects writers, creators, and their families and estates, being presented to a jury."Warner Bros has not yet commented on the latest ruling.

schema.headline: The Pitt and ER are similar enough for lawsuit to proceed, judge rules

title: Quentin Tarantino and Kylie Minogue film movie in Porthcawl
description: Sharing a pint with Reservoir Dogs and Pulp Fiction director Quentin Tarantino in his local pub was a surreal experience for a Welsh filmmaker.But thi
body: Sharing a pint with Reservoir Dogs and Pulp Fiction director Quentin Tarantino in his local pub was a surreal experience for a Welsh filmmaker.But this was just the tip of the iceberg for Jamie Adams, who also managed to get singing icon Kylie Minogue and rapper RZA from the Wu-Tang Clan to Porthcawl for his new movie.The arrival of the stars in the seaside town earlier this year to work on Tangled Up in Blue caused a buzz, and Adams admitted it felt like "an out of body experience" bringing his heroes to his hometown.It is not the first time he has brought big names to south Wales, having worked with Dirty Dancing star Jennifer Grey on 2019 film Bittersweet Symphony.Adams was able to include scenes in locations that mean a lot to him, including the pub his dad used to run."It was called the Ship and Castle then and the bar is actually a boat that he brought from Weymouth, which is where I was born," he said."So I've got Quentin Tarantino having a pint with me in my dad's old pub, talking to Neil, one of my old pals, who I've known since I was like eight years old."It's all very surreal and beautiful."Tangled Up in Blue follows a talent manager (Tarantino) who has spent 40 years managing legends but finds himself stranded at a hotel bar caught between an old flame and a lost soul.It all fell into place with the involvement of the superstars after Adams filmed in France in 2025.

schema.headline: Quentin Tarantino and Kylie Minogue film movie in Porthcawl

title: El Nino is making the Pacific 'burn with fever', triggering typhoon after typhoon in East Asia
description: Wild weather is a way of life for people living along the coast in the Philippines, Taiwan, China and Japan. But the last few months have been extraor
body: Wild weather is a way of life for people living along the coast in the Philippines, Taiwan, China and Japan. But the last few months have been extraordinary.A wave of intense and, at times, unpredictable storms exacerbated by the El Niño weather pattern has killed dozens, shuttered major airports and wiped out crops and infrastructure across a swathe of East Asia.In October, nearly all of Taiwan shut down as a monster storm big enough to engulf the island of 23 million roared towards its north-eastern coast. Equivalent to a category five hurricane, Typhoon Champi's 295km/h (193mph) winds had the power to flatten homes and whip up destructive waves.Thankfully it did not make landfall in Taiwan, skirting past the island while dousing it in rain. But it had far-reaching impacts: hundreds of flights were cancelled in Hong Kong, Taiwan and Japan. In the Philippines' Batanes archipelago, seaside highways shut as huge waves crashed onto the shore, and in southern Japan's Okinawa islands, power was cut to 15,000 homes.El Niño is a naturally occurring climate phenomenon in which warm waters pooling in the eastern Pacific and altered wind patterns drive extreme weather events around the world.It happens around every two to seven years, lasting for around a year. This year's El Niño, which the UK Met Office has forecast to be the "strongest in living memory", is likely to last until February or March.In June, Japan watched two storms - Typhoon Mekkhala and Severe Tropical Storm Higos - race towards its eastern coast simultaneously, forcing one million people to evacuate. In July, Tropical Storm Narra grazed China's southern coast along Guangxi, submerging villages and displacing tens of thousands.In August, Typhoon Chan-Hom baffled storm watchers in Japan by crossing the country from east to west, as opposed to the usual south-to-north trajectory. Japan's well-resourced and prepared authorities were able to evacuate people swiftly, but this would be far more challenging in some neighbouring countries.To get a better picture of how rising temperatures could amplify the risks, Manila-based climatologist Rafaela Jane Delfino and colleagues simulated the effects of warmer conditions on the Philippines' most recent monster storms, including 2013's Super Typhoon Haiyan (Yolanda) which killed more than 6,000 people. They arrived at what she describes as "very, very scary findings": higher temperatures increased total accumulated rainfall by 26%. It's a devastating prospect in a country where flooding from monsoon rains and some 20 tropical storms per year has emerged as one of the main disaster risks.In recent years, floods have paralysed entire cities for days, and tired of the annual ordeal, Filipinos have taken to the streets to protest against corruption which they say is gnawing away at millions of dollars from flood-control projects.Delfino, in an article on the University of the Philippines website, insists leaders and officials must gain a better understanding of climate hazards if communities are to be better prepared.

schema.headline: El Nino is making the Pacific 'burn with fever', triggering typhoon after typhoon in East Asia

title: Ranbir Kapoor in Ramayana: India's costliest film retells a beloved Hindu epic - but divides critics
description: Image source, Ramayana: Rise of a Legend, Sony PicturesImage caption, The film adapts the revered Hindu epic RamayanaByZoya MateenBBC News, DelhiIndia
body: Image source, Ramayana: Rise of a Legend, Sony PicturesImage caption, The film adapts the revered Hindu epic RamayanaByZoya MateenBBC News, DelhiIndia's most expensive film - a lavish retelling of the Hindu epic Ramayana, made in two parts for a reported $500m (£370m) - has opened in cinemas worldwide, sparking enormous expectations and mixed reviews.Directed by Nitesh Tiwari, Ramayana: Rise of a Legend is the first of two planned films, a sprawling production that brings together some of India's biggest stars, Hollywood visual-effects expertise and two Oscar-winning composers in an attempt to take one of the country's most revered stories to a global audience.One of Hinduism's foundational epics, the Ramayana has travelled across centuries and continents, finding expression in poetry, temple sculpture, shadow puppetry, folk theatre and stories passed down through generations. It has outlasted kingdoms and empires, inspired religious devotion and political movements, and found new life, again and again, on TV and in cinema.Tiwari's version returns to the familiar story of love, duty, exile and war, set in a world of gods and demons, celestial weapons and mighty kingdoms.Ranbir Kapoor plays Lord Ram, the virtuous prince of Ayodhya. Banished from his kingdom for 14 years, he retreats to the forest with his wife Sita (played by Sai Pallavi), who is kidnapped by Ravana, the 10-headed king of Lanka.Figure caption, Watch: Indian film star Ranbir Kapoor on AI, movies and fatherhoodPlayed by Yash, one of southern India's biggest stars, Ravana is a powerful warrior whose pride leads him into an epic battle with Ram (which will be depicted in part 2, set to release next year).The film's producer, Namit Malhotra, heads visual-effects company DNEG, which has worked on Hollywood blockbusters including Dune and Interstellar. The music is a collaboration between AR Rahman, the Oscar-winning Indian composer of Slumdog Millionaire, and Hans Zimmer, whose scores for Gladiator, The Dark Knight and Dune have helped define the sound of modern Hollywood.The film opened days ahead of Diwali, the Hindu festival of lights which celebrates Ram's return to Ayodhya after his exile.But the critical response so far has been mixed. Saibal Chatterjee of NDTV channel gave it, external three out of five stars, saying its visual spectacle often overshadowed the story. Its enormous scale, he wrote, "remains, for the most part, the only thing that stands out", while the acting remains "wildly inconsistent".Image source, Ramayana: Rise of a Legend, Sony PicturesImage caption, The film's release comes days ahead of Diwali, which celebrates Ram's return to Ayodhya and the "victory of good over evil"Rishabh Suri of the Hindustan Times newspaper was more enthusiastic, awarding it four stars. "I am happy to report, all that money shows on screen," he wrote, praising the performances and visual effects, though he found the first half sluggish and the music underwhelming.Shubhra Gupta, external of The Indian Express, who gave the film three stars, confessed to initial misgivings about its extravagant scale but found herself gradually won over, calling it the "perfect epic".There was "enough sorcery and thrills and adventure" to sustain the spectacle, she wrote, and the filmmakers had managed to tell a sprawling story without being swallowed by it.Internationally, too, the film drew contrasting reactions.Writing in The Guardian, Peter Bradshaw called it a "thoroughly engaging, rousing and spectacular Indian epic melodrama". He found echoes of Shakespeare in the royal intrigue that sends Rama into exile, and of Homer in his quest to rescue Sita. Its sweeping landscapes and fantastical imagery reminded him of The Lord of the Rings and The Lion King."It's a rather amazing adventure," he wrote, external, giving it four stars.Others were less impressed. Siddhant Adlakha of IGN scored the film four out of 10, describing its action as "clunky" and its computer-generated imagery as an "eye-sore".Image source, Ramayana: Rise of a Legend, Sony PicturesImage caption, Sita's abduction by Ravana sets off an epic battleGiovanni Lago of Next Best Picture, who gave it, external five out of 10, praised Yash's magnetic Ravana and the score by Rahman and Zimmer. But he felt the film's vast narrative might have been better served by a Game of Thrones-style series.The use of AI to adjust actors' lip movements for the English-language version also drew criticism. While Tiwari said it was intended to make the film more accessible to international audiences, Adlakha likened the result to "exaggerated mouth movements superimposed on still images for comedy sketches".In India, the film has invited comparisons with earlier adaptations, particularly Ramanand Sagar's Ramayan, which captivated the country nearly four decades ago with simple sets and special effects that now seem quaint.When the series first aired in 1987, Sunday mornings across India took on an almost devotional stillness.Streets emptied, shops lowered their shutters and neighbours crowded around TV sets. Some viewers bathed, lit incense and garlanded their screens before the broadcast, preparing for the show much as they might for worship.Arvind Rajagopal, a media scholar at New York University, told the BBC in 2019 that trains and buses would stop and passengers disembark to watch the show on roadside TVs.Broadcast on the state-run Doordarshan network, some of the most popular parts of the 78-episode series drew an estimated 80-100 million viewers, astonishing numbers at a time when owning a TV was a luxury in India.The actors, too, became objects of reverence. Arun Govil, who played Ram, has recalled people weeping at the sight of him and touching his feet. Now, in a casting choice brimming with nostalgia, Govil returns in Tiwari's film as Dasharatha, Ram's father.Image source, Ramanand Sagar ProductionsImage caption, Ramanand Sagar's Ramayan remains the most popular adaptation of the Hindu epic to dateOther adaptations found their own ways to reimagine the epic. The 1992 Indo-Japanese animated film Ramayana: The Legend of Prince Rama brought the tale to life through richly detailed, hand-drawn animation.Tiwari's Ramayana arrives with technological resources its predecessors could barely have imagined - but also with the expectations of generations who have grown up with the story and its characters. It also comes at a politically charged moment in India, where Ram has become a powerful symbol of Hindu identity - over the past decade and a half, even popular analyses or retellings of the epic have landed in controversy. The 2023 film Adipurush, another big-budget retelling of Ramayana, sparked backlash on several fronts. Hindu groups called for a ban, accusing it of disrespecting religious figures, while some critics questioned its depiction of Ravana, which they said drew on Mughal imagery and reinforced stereotypes about Muslims. The film was also criticised for its dialogue and visual effects.For the actors portraying these characters in the latest film, that burden was deeply felt."I was filled with fear," Kapoor told the BBC Asian Network's Haroon Rashid. "I knew that maybe I'm too old for this. I won't be able to do justice to it."He called the role "an opportunity of a lifetime", but said playing a figure worshipped by millions left little room for the creative freedom he had enjoyed in other films.Sai Pallavi, who plays Sita, said the experience was as much spiritual as artistic. Raised in a religious household, she said she approached the part not just as a performance, but as an opportunity for personal growth.How the film is being received will become clearer soon, as audiences head to cinemas.But whatever the verdict, it marks a major cultural moment for India, bringing a story loved for generations to the big screen on an unprecedented scale.

schema.headline: Ranbir Kapoor in Ramayana: India's costliest film retells a beloved Hindu epic - but divides critics

title: Jessica Pegula calls Mirra Andreeva 'diva' after Indian Wells practice session
description: World number five Jessica Pegula described Mirra Andreeva as "a diva" on a live stream after a practice session with the Russian teenager.In a private
body: World number five Jessica Pegula described Mirra Andreeva as "a diva" on a live stream after a practice session with the Russian teenager.In a private conversation with her coach Mark Knowles, American Pegula could be heard saying that French Open champion Andreeva "needs to be humbled" and that her coach Conchita Martinez encourages her behaviour.The session at Indian Wells, California, was live streamed by the Women's Tennis Association before the WTA Tour Finals start on Sunday.Pegula and Knowles remained on court after the session. The comments, which included some expletives from 32-year-old Pegula, were picked up by a courtside microphone.YouTube streams of practice sessions at Indian Wells have since been removed by the WTA, but footage has been shared on social media.Pegula, who is a member of the WTA players' council, also praised Andreeva, saying the world number three is "wonderful" and "smart".The season-ending WTA Finals, being held at Indian Wells for the first time, run until 15 November.Pegula's representative and the WTA have been approached for comment.In a separate incident, world number one Elena Rybakina appeared to have an angry exchange with her coach before a practice session with Wimbledon champion Linda Noskova.Some of the audio is unclear, but Pegula can be heard describing how Andreeva and Martinez complained throughout the session, even though Andreeva won every game.Knowles: "She treats Conchita so bad."Pegula: "Conchita's always been very nice to me, but I've lost a little respect for her because I'm like, this girl - I think she's a nice girl - she's just a diva. She needs to be humbled. She needs to be [inaudible] putting her in her place; [inaudible] stand up to her."Spaniard Martinez, the 1994 Wimbledon champion, began working with Andreeva in April 2024. Andreeva reached the Wimbledon quarter-finals last year and claimed her first Grand Slam title at Roland Garros in June.Pegula: "Conchita pokes her and eggs on her behaviour."Knowles: "She needs somebody to put her in her place. Once she gets that, I think she'll be really good. I mean, she's already really good. Look how she moves."Pegula: "She moves like a cat. She's wonderful. She's got the perfect serve. She's smart. She anticipates well."Pegula, who has not won a Grand Slam, then compared Andreeva to world number four Coco Gauff. The American was also 19 when she won her first Grand Slam. Now 22, she has won two majors.Pegula: "It's so funny how you see her and then you see Coco's mentality. If she had Coco's mentality, she'd be better than her."Knowles: "Oh, definitely."Pegula: "The serve, everything, all-around, and she moves just as good. But like mentally, she's..."Pegula and Andreeva are in different groups at the WTA Finals but could meet in the semi-finals or final.

schema.headline: Jessica Pegula calls Mirra Andreeva 'diva' after Indian Wells practice session

title: Interest rates hiked to 4% in first increase in over three years
description: Interest rates have risen for the first time in more than three years and the Bank of England has signalled a further increase is likely unless the US
body: Interest rates have risen for the first time in more than three years and the Bank of England has signalled a further increase is likely unless the US-Iran war is resolved.Rates rose to 4% from 3.75% in a bid to curb inflation mainly driven by the conflict's impact on oil prices.Andrew Bailey, the Bank's governor, said the decision "shouldn't be seen as the first in an inevitable long sequence of hikes", but warned "unless the conflict in the Middle East is resolved, neither does it seem likely to be the last increase".The higher level will increase the cost of borrowing for things such as mortgages, loans and credit cards, but will also lead to higher returns on savings.The Bank's rate-setting committee all backed increasing interest rates, with eight out of nine voting in favour of the rise to 4%. One member wanted an even bigger increase to 4.25%.Bailey said the rate hike was warranted due to higher energy prices, but stressed it was not the start of a series of rate rises.The governor pointed to what happens in the Middle East as the main factor in future decisions."Put simply, it requires real progress towards settling the conflict in the Middle East," he said.Bailey said he could "see the argument" for a further rate hike, before taking a "more conditional approach, dependent on the evidence on energy prices and inflation dynamics".However, members of the rate-setting committee offered different views on the path forward.Clare Lombardelli agreed there was "likely to be a case for a further increase in rates in the near term", but Megan Greene said any decision would depend on how inflation impacts wages, prices and the jobs market.Alan Taylor said the rate rise was a "a risk-management 'one-for-now' insurance hike".Brighton-based mortgage-holder Patrick Bryson is coming to the end of a five-year term with a 3.51% interest rate and said things are "100% getting tighter".The best deal the 51-year-old can find is a 5.17% loan with HSBC, which means his repayments will jump from £1,420 to £1,680 a month from February."The only thing that bugs me about the mortgage is that after five years of paying it off we are now paying more than we were before," said the father-of-three. "That's a bit of a slap in the face."Patrick, a guitar teacher, has a combined income of around £68,000 a year with his wife, who manages a care home.But he said the couple is already feeling the pressure of higher food prices and energy bills and will have to cut back.They have already started doing most of their shopping at Lidl, and Peter plans to ditch his £135-a-month broadband, TV streaming package for a cheaper option."Over the last year I have stopped buying wine, we don't go out to eat much anymore, we have knocked takeaways on the head. The prices are ridiculous," he said.The Bank now expects inflation to peak at 4.9% in the middle of next year, higher than it originally estimated, and not return to its target of 2% until 2028.In what it called an "adverse scenario", where the US-Iran war could escalate further and send oil and gas prices much higher, inflation could reach 6.2% in 2027, it suggested.While the UK cannot control global energy prices, the Bank is raising rates in order to limit the knock-on effects of high energy prices resulting in inflation going up across the board.

schema.headline: Interest rates hiked to 4% in first increase in over three years

title: Two more arrests following Chandler's Ford Halloween party stabbing
description: The officer leading the investigation, Det Ch Insp Elizabeth Pirie, said: "During an investigation like this one, information is provided to us which
body: The officer leading the investigation, Det Ch Insp Elizabeth Pirie, said: "During an investigation like this one, information is provided to us which will require us to make an arrest in order to secure possible evidence and take someone's account."We have been working closely with the CPS to assess the available evidence and review whether there is sufficient grounds for charges to be authorised or if there is additional enquiries which need to be made."Today, we have released two of the boys we have arrested on police bail while we continue with our investigation. This bail comes with strict conditions in place, and this is monitored to ensure those conditions are being complied with."Pirie said the force had a large number of officers working on the case as it tried to piece together the movements of those it believed were involved.  Hampshire Police is continuing to appeal for witnesses, and anyone who may have information, to come forward and has thanked those it has already spoken to.  Pirie added: "I know that for those who were at the party on Saturday, this has been a really distressing time, but their help has been so important."

schema.headline: Two more arrests following Chandler's Ford Halloween party stabbing

title: Would you take a test to see if your life will be cut short? I did - and it changed me
description: Image source, Katie DoyImage caption, Laura Sides faced a dilemma of whether to get tested to see if she had inherited her father's conditionByEmily D
body: Image source, Katie DoyImage caption, Laura Sides faced a dilemma of whether to get tested to see if she had inherited her father's conditionByEmily DoughtyIf you could find out if you had a gene that would cut your life short, would you?This is the dilemma Laura Sides faced when she was offered a test for the rare form of early onset dementia that her dad was diagnosed with in his 40s.Laura spoke to Dr Sian Williams, host of BBC Radio 4's Life Changing podcast, about her decision to take the test and how it has shaped the rest of her life.Growing up, Laura says she always felt close to her dad as they had a "similar nature". He was a GP and "the most amazing doting father," she says. When his Alzheimer's symptoms became more severe, Laura dropped out of university to care for him."We did have a really lovely time," she says, remembering trips to a lighthouse and collecting coasters. "I'd run him baths and just play music and pour jugs of hot water over his head and he loved it."Image source, Laura SidesImage caption, Laura had just celebrated her 21st birthday when she began caring for her dadIt was at a hospital appointment with her dad when a doctor told Laura she had a 50/50 chance of developing the same type of early onset Alzheimer's known as the "London variant". "All I could think was, that's a toss of a coin," she says. "I was still so involved with what was going on with him [her dad]. I just pushed it really, really deep down."Laura's dad died in 2009, just a year after her mum had died."All of a sudden I got such an overwhelming urge to leave," she says. So she booked a solo around-the-world trip, eventually settling in Melbourne, Australia.It was there that thoughts of inheriting her dad's condition "started creeping in" and she went to see a specialist in 2013. He told her a test could determine with 99.999% certainty if she would inherit early onset dementia. If she had the gene, her expected age of decline would be 46 to 48, he said."I just thought, I'm not there yet. I don't want to do that."Life Changing'Toss of a coin’ if I’d inherit dementia gene4 November 2026As Laura entered her 30s she found herself thinking about the test more and more and decided she wanted to know. But first, she had to undergo six months of genetic counselling."There's not many realms in life where you find out your fate and it can be very difficult information to process," she says.After a six-week wait for the test results to come through, the day finally arrived. Laura says she felt "extremely nervous". She had booked a table for lunch with a friend afterwards - but went into the appointment alone. "I said, 'Let's cut straight to it.' They said, 'We're really sorry, it's not good news, and you have inherited the gene.'" She remembers "almost a white blurry noise of just sitting there"."I came out of that room and my friend burst into hysterical tears." But Laura didn't react. "We went for our lunch and it was lovely. I don't know if it'd sunk in."The reality hit later. "I was angry. I felt it was so unjust. I was just too confused at how I was meant to live now. How do you live with that knowledge?"Image source, Laura SidesImage caption, Laura has taken part in medical trials all over the worldLaura began to feel a pull back home to the UK, especially as her sister was pregnant. "It doesn't make sense... to live on the other side of the world when she's going to have a baby."However, her around-the-world travels continued as she took part in medical trials before and after her diagnosis."It felt like such a positive to be involved in something out of such a negative situation."Image source, Laura SidesImage caption, Laura (right) is a chef and owns a cafe restaurant and catering business with two friendsLaura is now 43 - three years away from the age doctors predicted she will begin to notice symptoms."I keep waiting for something to sort of hit home. I guess one day I'll start declining but that doesn't keep me up at night."She is "grateful and so lucky for the people in her life". But meeting anyone new is hard. "Do I tell them? Do I not tell them? At what point do I tell them? "And more often than not, when I have told them, it ends." However she says she has been "proven wrong". "I have been shown I can be loved despite this. It fills my heart with reassurance and joy".  Laura says she had always "naively assumed" she would be a mother."[Its] one of the very few things that I never questioned that I'd be good at and I wanted to do. That's hard... but it doesn't make sense to do it. It wouldn't be fair."Image source, Laura SidesImage caption, Laura loves swimming and is aiming to swim in as many seas as possibleFor Laura, life is now about tapping in to things that "make her happy". "It's not about huge aspirations. It's not like I want to see the Grand Canyon... I want to have time now around the people that I adore and make me feel safe. "I love nature. I love being outside. I'm obsessed with being submerged in water. It sounds so corny, but...I believe it really is actually the little things are the big things."I hope I just have a wonderful few years in this world... drinking champagne and eating oysters - two of my favourite things."If you or someone you know has been affected by dementia, you can access support from the BBC Action Line.Get in touchHave you been affected by the issues raised in this story?Get our flagship newsletter with all the headlines you need to start the day. Sign up here.

schema.headline: Would you take a test to see if your life will be cut short? I did - and it changed me

title: Cristiano Ronaldo retirement: Why has Portugal legend retired from international game?
description: Cristiano Ronaldo's old rival Leo Messi left Argentina less than a month ago with a nation applauding him.The Portugal legend has gone another way, an
body: Cristiano Ronaldo's old rival Leo Messi left Argentina less than a month ago with a nation applauding him.The Portugal legend has gone another way, and it was always going to be the case.The 41-year-old announced his international retirement after 23 years but also after a fallout with coach Jorge Jesus which was resolved with a sanction of 30 days, that had already been served, and a fine of 255 euros.It was the punishment imposed on the Portuguese striker for leaving the team's training camp without permission. Jesus kept him on the bench for one match and said he did not plan to start him in the next, so Ronaldo went home.His last appearance came on 24 September against Wales. He ends his international career with 146 goals in 234 games.A message went around Portugal with a big thank you for everything, calling Ronaldo a global ambassador and an inspiration to millions. Even so, the way it ended leaves a bit of a bitter taste.Was he going to be named in the next squad? Possibly, as Jesus said the door was open and the decision was Ronaldo's. What is clear is that he was no longer an automatic starter, and Cristiano has never handled that well.So is this another hissy fit? Partly, yes. He reacted the way he always has when a coach questions his place. But the label hides how much he adapted over the years.Such a pattern appears with almost every man who sat on the Portuguese bench - there were clashes, but also communion with managers and team-mates that help explain this ending.When a young Ronaldo first joined the squad, he arrived at camp with his baseball cap on backwards, enormous sunglasses and headphones turned up so loud they could be heard from a distance.He would not take the cap off to eat among veterans like Luis Figo and Rui Costa. Luiz Felipe Scolari saw an extraordinary player who was immature and obsessed with showing off. He reprimanded him in public, then told him privately that if he changed his attitude, he would one day captain Portugal.The first great disappointment came early, and it came at home. At 19, Ronaldo played in the final of Euro 2004 at the Estadio da Luz in Lisbon, in front of a country that had convinced itself the trophy was already on its way.A single headed goal by Angelos Charisteas was enough for unfancied Greece to win it by surprise. When the final whistle went, Ronaldo could not hold back the tears, and the image of the teenager crying on his own pitch travelled everywhere.It was a painful way to learn what a final costs, and it left him with a hunger that never really went away.Figo owned the number 7 at the time, so Ronaldo had to have 17. Figo helped him settle but had no intention of making it easy. When he left the national team in 2006, the shirt and the team became Ronaldo's.In September 2005, before a qualifier in Russia, Scolari and Figo went to his room to tell him his father had died. Scolari offered to send him home. Ronaldo chose to play, asked his team-mates to behave as normal, and spent time in the dressing room doing ball tricks.That was his way to cope with the expected but still hugely hurtful passing of his alcoholic dad.  He later called Scolari "father". That way the national team had become the place that held him together.Things went sour with Carlos Queiroz. After the 2010 World Cup exit against Spain, asked to explain a poor performance, Ronaldo told journalists to ask the coach. His influence in the camp had grown so large it changed routines and habits, which explains why the coach felt undermined.The sociologist Joao Nuno Coelho offers the best lens on how Portugal sees him. In his analysis, the national team became a representation of Portuguese identity and of the country's need to be seen internationally.In years of economic hardship and a crisis of confidence, a team that won admiration abroad was important beyond football.Ronaldo stood at the centre of that need and created contradictory feelings. Some Portuguese questioned his individualism and his ego, and not everyone saw themselves in his personality.Coelho explains criticising him became more difficult as time went by. The country wanted to be proud of him and sometimes felt uneasy at the same time.The former international Jorge Andrade told me some supporters preferred figures like Figo, Eusebio, Paulo Futre or Rui Costa. Even so, Portugal was proud to have him. And with the titles, the doubts eased.Under Fernando Santos in 2016, he changed. He accepted playing as a centre forward next to Nani - he had never taken a coach's instructions so naturally.After the opening draw with Iceland, he told Nani in private that he trusted Santos, and the dressing room began to see a real captain. After missing a penalty against Austria, he barely slept. Santos woke up and found him already awake.At the training camp in Marcoussis, he took a fan's megaphone and told supporters Portugal had won nothing yet. He was enjoying the leadership role.In the final in Paris, he left the pitch in tears, injured. He had not had the best tournament, with a muscle complaint that did not let him perform at his best.Nani took the armband. At half-time Ronaldo pulled himself together to encourage his team-mates, and before extra time, still limping, he told Eder he would score.And Eder did.But the old instinct never fully disappeared. During extra-time, Ronaldo stood in the technical area giving orders until the fourth official sent him back. Other coaches I consulted found it excessive.His greatest strength, the need to influence every result, also made limits hard to accept.When he debuted in 2003, Portugal was still searching for its first major title. Some players mark an era, and others change a national team for good. He belongs to the second group.That night in July 2016 gave Portugal its first European Championship.Three years later he scored a hat-trick against Switzerland to put them into the first Nations League final, which Portugal won. In 2025 he lifted a second Nations League at an age when most players have retired.No one has scored more goals for a national side, and no one has pulled on the Portugal shirt more times.Under his influence, Portugal stopped being a gifted team and became one that arrives at every tournament expecting to contend, while a whole generation of players came through a dressing room where he decided what the standard was.Coelho's point holds here as well: a small country found a way to be noticed, and for two decades he was its face.After 2016 the question around him changed. Fewer asked whether he was selfish, and more asked whether Portugal depended on him too much.In the World Cup in 2018, he scored three against Spain, including a free-kick after 45 attempts in major tournaments, and the team still went out to Uruguay.After a difficult 2026 World Cup, much was made of him still starting up front when in fact statistically that was his best period.Under Roberto Martinez, with 28 goals in 37 games, 0.756 per match, improves the 0.624 with Santos.The federation has announced a special tribute to honour his contribution, and that is necessary as the exit has not left fans room for a celebration they want to be part of.Not only they grew up with him, he took them to places they had not yet been.

schema.headline: Cristiano Ronaldo retirement: Why has Portugal legend retired from international game?

title: Could this be the last Bonfire Night for noisy fireworks?
description: Bangers, rockets and screamers have long been part of Bonfire Night - but the traditional celebrations might sound a little different next year.The go
body: Bangers, rockets and screamers have long been part of Bonfire Night - but the traditional celebrations might sound a little different next year.The government is currently considering reducing the noise limit for fireworks by 50% for those bought in shops for private use, after pressure from campaigners concerned about the impact on nervous animals and people with Post Traumatic Stress Disorder (PTSD).Professionally organised displays would continue to have no maximum limit provided the noise level is not harmful to human health.About 20 million people enjoy fireworks at home every year, according to industry figures.Andy Hubble, of the British Fireworks Association (BFA), said displays had already been getting quieter and a balance must be struck to prevent a black market in noisy fireworks springing up.The end of October sees the start of several celebrations traditionally marked by fireworks and bonfires, including Halloween on 31 October, Guy Fawkes Night on 5 November, and Diwali, which is on 8 November this year.The government has said an outright ban on the public buying fireworks would not be proportionate.But Business Minister Kate Dearden said her department was considering "reforms to fireworks legislation, focused on their key harms associated with their misuse - their noise, and contribution to antisocial behaviour – whilst still allowing individuals to enjoy fireworks safely and responsibly for the important community and cultural celebrations they play a part of."It is already illegal to sell fireworks to under 18s, or to set fireworks off after 23:00, with exemptions for special occasions including Bonfire Night, Diwali, New Year's Eve and Chinese New Year.But campaigners have raised concerns about the impact of loud bangs on nervous pets.Dog owner Katherine Alderson, from Clacton-on-Sea, told BBC Breakfast: "It's a nightmare every single year."This year I've actually barricaded my bedroom window with numerous layers of insulation to try and keep out the noise of fireworks."Asked whether reducing the bangs would take the fun out of fireworks, she said she believed displays "should be about the lights and colours" and suggested "a complete ban" on the sale of fireworks to the general public could be the solution.But other campaigners say a ban is not needed, including Alan Friggieri, from the charity Combat Stress, which supports veterans with PTSD.Giving evidence to MPs on the Commons' Business Committee, Friggieri said calls to their helpline jump at this time of year because loud bangs can trigger PTSD symptoms."Nothing quite sounds like an AK47 other than fireworks going off - it's that crackle," one veteran who had been shot multiple times had told him.Friggieri said veterans need to be able to plan around key dates, but he said he was not calling for a ban, because his organisation understands the cultural importance of firework displays.Calling for better enforcement of existing rules by police to stop antisocial behaviour, BFA vice chairman Hubble warned a ban in Ireland had seen a flourishing black market in firework sales. "There is a real risk here that if we make fireworks quieter that there is still a demand then we could create an illegal market where fireworks are coming in through internet sales and white van sales," he told BBC Breakfast."At the moment we have a really well-regulated market where we have enforcers that know the products and can test them but as soon as these products go undercover then we lose that."We could actually create a louder and noisier environment because those are the sorts of fireworks that we're seeing coming in through illegal sales on the internet."Asked whether it was true that displays were getting noisier, Hubble said: "No, no, it's a lot quieter than it used to be - we used to have bangers and air bombs and and screamer rockets that used to be on sale and they were withdrawn from sale."The government is considering reducing the maximum noise limit from the current 120dB, equivalent toa thunderclap, to 110dB, which is equivalent to a car horn. Hubble said a BFA assessment of firework sales shows a 50% noise reduction to 110 dB would impact up to 60% of firework sales to the general public. Lowering levels to 90DB, equivalent to a lawnmower, as some campaigners want, would affect about 95% of fireworks."That's effectively a ban on consumer fireworks, not a modest reduction in noise," he said.RSPCA advice for people with nervous pets:Stay calm and show your pet that all is wellPut on music or the TV to help mask firework soundsClose any windows and do what you can to block out both the noise and the flashesKeep your environment secure: make sure your pet can't escape if there's a sudden noiseFor dogs: let them pace around, if they're whining, barking or hiding, let themPlay with a toy if your pet wants to join in, but don't force them to playCombat Stress advice for people with PTSD:Use noise cancelling headphones to reduce the sound of explosions and blackout blinds to block out  flashes of lightUse scented candles, diffusers or plug ins to make your home smell good and nothing like those you remember from deploymentsRemind yourself you are safe, and focus on the present using breathing and grounding techniques, or with exerciseAsk friends and family to be with you on key dates like Bonfire Night

title: Vance walks Trump tightrope with scathing election critique blaming Iran war
description: Figure caption, With Congress flipped, what does Donald Trump do next?ByWashington correspondentUpdated 03:47 GMTVice-President JD Vance sent shockwav
body: Figure caption, With Congress flipped, what does Donald Trump do next?ByWashington correspondentUpdated 03:47 GMTVice-President JD Vance sent shockwaves through Washington on Wednesday by blaming his party's midterm defeat squarely on the Iran war, in what was widely interpreted as an effort to distance himself from President Donald Trump ahead of a potential 2028 White House run.In a carefully calibrated, 600-word statement on X, the vice-president acknowledged that Trump's 2024 voters had deserted Republicans in the midterm election."The reason we lost is the war," he wrote. "The president himself said so last night."In interviews late Tuesday night and Wednesday, Trump had defended the war but acknowledged that it played a factor in Democrats flipping control of the US House of Representatives and the Senate.Vance's view on the war in Iran is an open secret in Washington.  While he has repeatedly backed the conflict since the US and Israel attacked Tehran in February, he has reportedly expressed opposition in private meetings with administration officials.But those disagreements had been kept out of the public eye - until now.Figure caption, Could Democrats in Congress end the war in Iran?Hours after Trump and the party were handed a bruising election defeat, Vance made clear that he felt the decision to go to war was a clear political mistake."If you'd like to argue it was worth it, that losing the Senate for the next 6 years was worth it, then do so. Argue it was a worthwhile cost to pay. Agree or disagree, that's at least honest," Vance said.It was a striking statement, and one with no recent precedent: it's hard to recall a similar moment in recent US political history when a sitting vice-president has so sharply broken with the president on a signature foreign policy issue.Then came an arguably even greater surprise: Trump - who typically demands steadfast loyalty from his senior advisers - agreed with Vance that the midterms were "largely" decided by the war. He added that he would "do it again" if given the same choices.Image source, ReutersDrawing contrasts with Trump will be a delicate balancing act if Vance seeks the presidency, Byman added.That balance was on display in Vance's post. The vice president didn't mention Trump by name and attributed much of his election results analysis to unnamed pollsters.Vance "put his toe in the water to see what he's going to do," Ashley Davis, a Republican strategist, told the BBC.Beyond the Iran war criticism, Vance also offered a political roadmap that could preview a possible presidential campaign. He distilled the party's strategy to win back voters into a neat four-point gameplan:  "1) End the war 2) Focus on cost of living/inflation 3) Put America First 4) Change our relationship to Israel."The list encapsulated much of Vance's worldview since bursting onto the national political scene, and read like the core argument in a future stump speech.The BBC has contacted Vance's office for comment.Of course, the next presidential election is still two years away. Vance is expected to run but hasn't made an official decision, and aides insist that he's still mulling it over.It's also up for debate exactly how much Vance broke from Trump. Vance showed the message to Trump before posting it online, according to The New York Times.Trump, for his part, could change his mind and make clear he'll brook no dissent from Vance or anyone else.The president has been circumspect about who he'd support to succeed him as the 2028 Republican presidential nominee. Trump has praised Vance and Secretary of State Marco Rubio on several occasions, but hasn't said when - or if – he'd make an endorsement.The president appears to relish the guessing game of who he'd back to carry on his political movement, even in the past floating the idea that he'd continue to a third term (which is barred by the US Constitution).Vance's midterms missive might not be that significant in the end. Or it could have been the starting gun for the 2028 race and the battle for the post-Trump Republican Party.Nardine Saad contributed reporting.

schema.headline: Vance walks Trump tightrope with scathing election critique blaming Iran war

title: Jesus de Miguel: Funeral of Tenerife forward takes place as family thankful for support
description: Jesus de Miguel's family said "the mark he has left on so many people" is something they will always remember as the footballer's funeral took place o
body: Jesus de Miguel's family said "the mark he has left on so many people" is something they will always remember as the footballer's funeral took place on Thursday.The Tenerife forward, who was 30, died after suffering a serious injury during a Spanish second division match on Monday.After colliding with the FC Andorra goalkeeper, De Miguel lay motionless on the pitch while being treated by medical staff and was taken to hospital, where the father-of-one died at 07:00 GMT on Tuesday.Goalkeeper Jesus Owono was sent off for the challenge and the game was abandoned.In the hours after the death was announced, mourners laid flowers and lit candles beneath a black and white image of De Miguel at the Estadio Heliodoro Rodriguez Lopez - the stadium on the island of Tenerife, where Monday's game took place.Tributes have been paid to De Miguel, who joined Tenerife in the summer of 2025, with a minute's silence being held at all games in European competitions this week.His agent, Manuel Hernandez, issued a statement on behalf of the family, which read: "Thank you for loving him, for remembering him and for being with us."We cannot find enough words to thank you for every message, every phone call and every gesture of affection we are receiving."Feeling such affection for Jesus and seeing the mark he has left on so many people is something we will always carry with us."Jesus leaves a void that is impossible to fill, but also cherished memories for all of us who were fortunate enough to share our lives with him."In a statement issued by his club Andorra on Wednesday, goalkeeper Owono said he is experiencing "the most difficult days of my life"."I feel enormous pain over the loss of Jesus," he added. "I think of him, his family, and everyone who loved him."De Miguel's funeral was held in his parents' hometown of Navahermosa, Toledo, about 125km from the Spanish capital Madrid.Current Spain coach Luis de la Fuente was among the mourners, along with Real Madrid president Florentino Perez, Atletico Madrid chief executive Miguel Angel Gil Marin and former Real and Spain coach Jose Antonio Camacho.The family also asked "with the utmost respect, that our privacy - and that of everyone who is supporting us at this time - be respected"."We need to grieve in the peace and quiet that this situation demands," the statement added."We appreciate the affection, concern and expressions of support that his loss is inspiring, and we are deeply grateful to you all."

schema.headline: Jesus de Miguel: Funeral of Tenerife forward takes place as family thankful for support

title: Stonehenge Altar Stone remains a mystery as theory overturned
description: Pirrie said his latest publication on the Altar Stone has "built the clearest picture yet" and was "the most comprehensive geological investigation of
body: Pirrie said his latest publication on the Altar Stone has "built the clearest picture yet" and was "the most comprehensive geological investigation of the Altar Stone ever undertaken".Professor Nick Pearce from Aberystwyth University, who worked on the previous research, said "ruling out potential source areas is just as important as identifying new ones". The geochemistry expert said: "Every location eliminated narrows the search and brings us closer to discovering where the Altar Stone originated."The stone is unique among those at Stonehenge, and tracing its source would provide valuable new insights into its remarkable journey to Salisbury Plain thousands of years ago."The world-famous Wiltshire monument was constructed in multiple phases between 3000 and 1600BC. However, not all stones come from the area.The smaller bluestones travelled around 225km from west Wales with research suggesting a few were taken directly from another circle.

title: Married at First Sight UK cancelled after BBC revealed rape allegations
description: Married at First Sight UK will not return, Channel 4 has said, following a BBC investigation into the hit reality TV show.The Channel 4 show was plung
body: Married at First Sight UK will not return, Channel 4 has said, following a BBC investigation into the hit reality TV show.The Channel 4 show was plunged into crisis earlier this year, after Panorama revealed rape allegations from two female cast members on the show, while a third woman alleged a non-consensual sex act. The men involved have denied all the allegations against them.A review was commissioned by Channel 4 shortly after the BBC first contacted the broadcaster, with details of the allegations we had heard.On Thursday, the completed review recommended extra safeguards on the show. But Channel 4 said the programme had "run its course" and apologised to the women involved in the investigation.The broadcaster's chief executive Priya Dogra said she was "very sorry for the distress those women have clearly felt", adding that the show's budget would be reinvested in "distinctive new programming".The Panorama investigation in May, in which three women made allegations about the men they were partnered with - claims the men deny, made the following allegations:One woman said her onscreen husband raped her and threatened her with an acid attack.A second woman told both Channel 4 and CPL, before broadcast, about being allegedly raped by her onscreen husband. Her episodes were still aired.A third woman - Shona Manderson, the only woman who was identified - accused her onscreen husband of sexual misconduct.All three women accused the show of not doing enough to protect them.Lawyers for CPL, the independent production company that makes the UK version of the show, previously said its welfare system is "gold standard" and industry-leading, and that it acted appropriately in all these cases.Channel 4 had initially told Panorama that all the allegations were "wholly uncorroborated".Dame Caroline Dinenage MP, chair of the House of Commons culture and media committee, said the decision to axe the show "makes sense" given the review's findings and the "seriousness of the allegations". "Reality TV contestants have often been treated as a commodity, with duty of care a slogan rather than a genuine principle. Everyone involved in producing and regulating reality TV must now learn and act," she added. A spokesman for Ofcom said the broadcast regulator would "carefully consider the reports published today as we move to strengthen our guidance for broadcasters". "We are clear that broadcasters have a duty of care towards members of the public who participate in their programmes."What is your reaction to the cancellation of MAFS UK?The review into the show was split into two - one part examined welfare protocols on MAFS UK, and the other reported on how Channel 4 handled the allegations.The review into welfare protocols, led by former BBC One Controller Lorraine Heggessey, concluded that some parts of the programme's format increased "the risk profile of the show".Although she found the protocols for MAFS UK were extremely thorough and of a high standard, she said "intimacy is a key focus", and that "some elements of the show could implicitly put pressure on contributors to be intimate".Heggessey made suggestions including installing CCTV in all areas of the apartments, constantly monitored by a welfare team, with panic buttons and "safe words" in place.She concluded that, with enhancements to the existing welfare framework and adjustments to the format, it would have been reasonable to continue to produce future series of MAFS UK.Speaking to BBC Radio 4's PM programme on Thursday, she added that the suggested changes "would have, in lots of ways, changed both the format and the nature of the show, but would have given the kind of protection that both Channel Four and CPL would have ideally looked for  to ensure the safety of all contributors".But she added that she "completely understood" why Dogra "decided that she doesn't want to proceed with it". The other part of the review, by law firm Clyde & Co, found that Channel 4 and CPL's welfare protocols were compliant with Ofcom's broadcasting code. There were no findings of a breach of the code regarding the handling of issues raised at the relevant times.But it said there were "a small number of instances" where the show's protocols had not been fully applied.This included one incident when "some contributors contravened the Code of Conduct relating to prohibited substances but were given a first and final warning rather than being removed from the programme".It added that Channel 4 and CPL could have undertaken a more structured longer-term review over multiple series. The review also made recommendations for areas where the contributor welfare framework could be "further strengthened". Dogra said welfare across all of their programmes is "a primary concern".She said that considering the "wholesale implementation" of the recommendations "provoked fundamental questions about the editorial proposition of a show that, I believe, has now run its course over 10 years".She added that the review "did not have the authority to adjudicate on the very serious allegations made by three women in the Panorama programme". Billed as a "bold social experiment", Married at First Sight UK - known to many as MAFS - sees single people agree to "marry" total strangers, after meeting for the first time at their mock weddings.The marriages are not legally binding, but viewers see the couples go on honeymoon, before moving in together and navigating their relationships - all while being filmed, almost every day.The UK version, which had been running for 10 seasons, is one of Channel 4's biggest shows, with audience figures often topping three million.Following the Panorama broadcast, Channel 4's chief executive Priya Dogra initially didn't apologise, although she did express her "sympathy" for those who had spoken up.Less than 48 hours later, she changed position, telling reporters she was "deeply sorry" over the women's distress.The impact of the Panorama progamme was swift, and sizeable.Channel 4 launched its external review, all the episodes were taken down from its streaming service, and a major sponsor pulled out.Married at First Sight UK usually starts airing in September, but the new series was put on hold following the revelations in the Panorama.Ofcom has since launched an investigation, and in June, a male cast member was arrested on suspicion of rape.The individual is not being named. The alleged victim is also not being named; anyone who makes an allegation of rape is entitled to anonymity by law.If you have more information about this story, you can reach Noor by email at noor.nanji@bbc.co.uk

title: South Wales Metro £200m tram-trains sit barely used for three years
description: £200m taxpayer-funded trains sit barely used for three yearsImage source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Transport for Wales say the tram‑trains are "cent
body: £200m taxpayer-funded trains sit barely used for three yearsImage source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Transport for Wales say the tram‑trains are "central" to delivering the faster, more frequent journeys on the South Wales MetroByDaniel DaviesWales political correspondentPeter Shuttleworth and Ben SummerBBC WalesUpdated 9 hours agoA new fleet of publicly funded trains that cost more than £200m still remain mostly unused more than three years after the first one was delivered.They were initially promised to be fully up and running by 2022 but Transport for Wales' (TfW) boss has said he expects all of the tram-trains will be in full service by the end of 2027.Data obtained by the BBC reveals that less than half of the 36 fleet - what TfW call the "final piece" in their £2bn South Wales Metro project - have passed rigorous statutory testing.TfW chief executive James Price said he wants trains that work "100% well, 100% of the time" before putting them into full service.Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, King Charles took the controls of a tram-train during a visit to officially open the new South Wales Metro depot that will store the new fleetTfW's flagship scheme to transform an old Victorian railway into a turn-up-and-go rapid transit service, similar to the London Underground and Manchester Metrolink, is Wales' single-biggest infrastructure project since devolution in 1999.It has been hit by delays and rising costs and the Welsh government-owned rail operator has missed numerous self-imposed targets to bring the tram-trains into full service across the south Wales valleys.Officially known as Class 398 Citylink multiple units, they were ordered from Swiss manufacturer Stadler in 2018 and the first arrived in Wales in March 2023.Image caption, Some of the South Wales Metro tram-trains have been stored at Transport for Wales' new £100m depot near Cardiff for up to three-and-a-half yearsThe King and former Prime Minister Keir Starmer have been on one but barely any passengers have.Six tram-trains, worth about £8m each which can run both on urban streets and rail, are currently in passenger testing across the valleys network.But they have been temporarily removed from service on occasions for what TfW described as "teething issues" and "early reliability challenges" because of "software" problems.Commuters have now been told they will not be fully in service across the whole 105-mile (170km) network until 2027 - five years later than originally promised."It's definitely frustrating," said Price."Everyone would want something to work first time, wouldn't they? It's frustrating but not unexpected."Passengers have been told the doubling of services from two to four trains an hour will be complete between Cardiff and Aberdare, Merthyr Tydfil and Treherbert by the end of 2027 - a pledge passengers were also initially told would happen by 2022.Commuters on those routes have had new trains since 2024 when TfW introduced their class 756 units onto the old valley line after years of delays and complaints about old rolling stock. "They got delivered earlier and the reliability was better," said Price."That meant that we weren't able to test the trams against the original date. The key thing for me was getting new trains into service and maximising value for money."Sixteen of TfW's 36 tram-train fleet have passed testing to ensure the three-carriage units are safe to run on the UK rail network - with 20 yet to complete the scrutiny required by the rail regulator.Image caption, The South Wales Metro is on the old Taff Vale Railway network that once transported coal from the south Wales coalfields to Cardiff Docks where it was then shipped around the worldThose tests on some of the vehicles started in 2024 - and data obtained by the BBC via a Freedom of Information (FOI) request shows they can take anything between six weeks and two years."Trains are not a mass-produced vehicle and you only experience problems when you bring them into service," said Price."I don't accept there is a problem with the tram-trains but the biggest issue is a software issue. That's because the whole fleet is controlled by one big software package and we've tried to automate as much of the train as we can."The good thing when automation is fully working, any improvements we make with the trains can be delivered through software rather than hard engineering."That will be cheaper, quicker and more reliable because if you do it on one train, all the other trains will behave in the same way."Figure caption, £200m of new tram-trains have been delivered in Wales, so why are most of them still not carrying passengers?TfW said they did not launch the tram-trains with a "big fanfare" and opted for a customer testing approach as they feared they "might come out of service"."What we want is trains that work 100% of the time, 100% well," said Price. "We've been achieving 95% on-time reliability on the valleys network and that's the high standard we want to achieve before bringing something into passenger service in large numbers."Image source, Transport for WalesImage caption, The first South Wales Metro tram-train arrived at TfW's depot on 21 March 2023 after months of testing at Network Rail's Rail Innovation and Development Centre in LeicestershirePrice said he met Stadler's chief executive recently in Germany for talks in a bid to speed up the tram-train rollout.Stadler has said it was "working closely" with TfW to address "minor issues" in what they described "one of the UK's most advanced battery tram-trains"."Testing and validation activities have progressed in phases, resulting in the identification and implementation of normal refinements, including software updates, as part of the fleet introduction process," a spokesperson said.TfW also said part of the delay is because the line electrification infrastructure was only finished in March because of hold ups caused by Covid and supply chain impact caused by the Ukraine war.Image source, Geograph | Gareth JamesImage caption, Before the new South Wales Metro rolling stock arrived, old Pacer trains like this Arriva Trains Wales unit were among the trains that served passengers in south WalesBut one railway expert reckons the tram-trains are maybe just too complicated."It's a pretty ambitious project," said rail engineer and broadcaster Gareth Dennis."The challenge of having such complicated trains trying to do everything to reduce the cost of the infrastructure requires a lot of stuff to be working on the train. All of that has to be tested to make sure it always works."The line infrastructure will tell the trains what to do through a series of beacons and TfW claim the South Wales Metro will be one of the most technologically advanced railway networks when the tram-trains are in full service.While 100% of the network is fully electrified, only two-thirds has traditional overhead electric wires.Image source, Transport for WalesImage caption, The 105-mile (170km) South Wales Metro is sometimes known as the 'Welsh Tube' or 'Tiwb Cymru' and has services with level boarding, has tap-in tap-out ticketing and multi-coloured linesBy not electrifying the entire track and using on-board batteries for non-electrified sections, TfW say they had saved about £400m and years of time.But Dennis fears the tram-trains are "being delivered as part of cutting some corners" like not doing complete overhead wire electrification" as he believes TfW try to get new services delivered quicker."It is the case that this is the first deployment that has pulled all this stuff together - being a tram, a train, having a battery and discontinuous electrification," added the host of the #railnatter podcast."But that isn't necessarily a very good idea and that's why it's not common."But TfW have said that technology already works on the bigger 756 trains, the temporary stop-gap before the purpose-built tram-trains are rolled out, and the project has won an industry award, external.Image caption, Transport for Wales say it can cut journey time from the top of the south Wales valleys to Cardiff to 50 minutes.Opposition politicians in Wales have questioned why most of the tram-trains were "just sitting in a depot gathering dust"."Taxpayers deserve to know what has gone wrong, how delays have turned into years and the costs are spiralling out of control," said Reform's transport spokesperson Jason O'Connell.TfW, who took over the running of the £5bn Wales and Borders franchise during Covid, said their south Wales valleys upgrades had been "quick"."If you think we didn't get hold of the lines until 2021 and by 2025 most of the work was substantially complete," said Price."And today we basically have 100% new trains - it's not as quick as we originally said but compared to any other project in the UK, it's very quick."Image caption, Once the tram-trains are in full service on the South Wales Metro, the class 756 trains that are currently operating on the network will move to their intended home on the Bridgend-Rhymney lineTfW have said introducing the tram-trains fully into service and operating four trains an hour on the three lines between Cardiff and Aberdare, Merthyr Tydfil and Treherbert is the "final piece of the South Wales Metro jigsaw"."The reason for, I guess, the relatively slow pace is that we need to train quite a few hundred crew then do signalling work at Queen Street station in Cardiff," said Price."I do fully expect to see four trains an hour by the end of next year definitely. If we can do it earlier, we certainly will do that."The Welsh government said TfW had already delivered "transformative improvements on the valleys network" and new trains would eventually "unlock turn-up-and-go" services across the valleys and Cardiff."Whilst some issues have delayed the introduction of the new tram trains TfW remains on target to complete the full rollout by the end of next year," it added.Get our flagship newsletter with all the headlines you need to start the day. Sign up here.
